chunks: Common decoupling capacitor values. The question: What are some common values for decoupling capacitors?

The usual decoupling value is 100 nanofarads at every supply pin, with a family of other values around it: a few nF or smaller for very high frequencies, 1 microfarads and 10 microfarads for middle frequencies, and large bulk capacitors near the regulator.
You need a family because every real capacitor also has a little inductance.
Above a certain frequency, its self-resonant frequency, it behaves like an inductor instead of a capacitor. Each value works best in its own frequency band.
Think of the gears on a bicycle. A low gear is great for climbing but useless at speed, and a high gear is the reverse.
Capacitor values are gears: big values work at low frequencies, small ones reach higher. Together they cover the range.
The analogy breaks in one place: above about 50 to 100 megahertz all the capacitors behave alike, so you need less inductance, not another value.
Each value is the lowest-impedance option only in its own band: 10 microfarads below ~2 megahertz, 1 microfarads to ~6 megahertz, 100 nanofarads to ~20 megahertz, 10 nanofarads to ~70 megahertz.
Above about 50 megahertz all of them climb along nearly the same inductive line (set by ESL, not C), so you need lower inductance , not other values.
ESR and ESL are representative; real parts differ.
ESL: equivalent series inductance, the small inductance built into every capacitor and its connections ("Realistic capacitor model and parasitics").
Self-resonant frequency: f 0 equals 1 over (2 pi square root of ESL times C ) .
Below it the part acts as a capacitor, above it as an inductor ("Capacitor self-resonant frequency").
Impedance: how much the part opposes a changing current at a given frequency, in ohms. Lower is better here.
DC-bias derating: ceramic capacitors lose capacitance as the steady voltage across them rises.
Bulk capacitor: a large capacitor near the regulator for slow changes in load ("What is bulk capacitance?")
Assume a typical 0. 5 nanohenries of ESL. A 100 nanofarads capacitor resonates at 1 over (2 pi square root of 0. 5 nanohenries times 100 nanofarads ) about 22. 5 megahertz.
A 1 microfarads part resonates at about 7. 1 megahertz, and a 10 nanofarads part at about 71 megahertz. Ten times more capacitance moves the resonance down by about three times.
Above resonance the impedance is 2 pi f times ESL , about 0. 31 ohms at 100 megahertz whatever the capacitance. That is the whole idea.
"The standard is 100 nanofarads ceramic, X7R or X5R, at every supply pin, because its self-resonance is around 20 megahertz and it covers the first tens of nanoseconds of a burst.
Around it, 10 nanofarads or smaller for higher frequency, 1 to 10 microfarads for the mid range, and 47 to 470 microfarads bulk near the regulator.
You need a range of values because each capacitor's parasitic inductance makes it inductive above its self-resonance.
I check the dielectric and the DC-bias derating, and follow the part's datasheet."
